title: When I See You Smile: Links Among Experienced Affect, Expressed Emotional Components, and Target Readability in a Supportive Interaction
abstract: ABSTRACT Navigating supportive interactions is an important task of friendship that involves exchanging affective information. However, experienced affect is not always readable, and emotional expressions are not all equally helpful in conveying experienced affect. We examined associations between target readability (i.e., emotional expressive accuracy, or the degree to which individuals accurately communicate their experienced affect to others), and experienced and expressed emotional components (i.e., facial expressions and affect words), when seeking support from a friend. Participants ( N = 137 dyads, M age = 19.61 years, SD age = 1.34 years) took turns discussing problems they were having. To measure experienced affect, participants reported their positive and negative affect during the interaction. Expressed emotional components were participants' facial movements (i.e., eyebrow movements and smiles) and use of positive and negative affect words. To measure readability, observers continuously rated participants' affect during the interaction; their ratings were correlated with similar self‐ratings made by participants, and those correlations were averaged. Participants were more readable when they reported experiencing greater negative affect. In terms of expressed emotional components, participants were more readable when they had more eyebrow raises, and fewer eyebrow furrows and smiles. Results elucidate factors that contribute to effective communication of experienced affect when seeking support from friends.
